transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-18 15:30 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Avery Kim (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Nimbus Head of ML), Tom Ruiz (Nimbus Platform Eng), Jordan Miles (CTO)

[00:00] Avery Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, audio ok?
[00:12] Sara Patel: Yep loud and clear, thanks.
[00:18] Marcus Li: Good afternoon. I'll share the pilot dashboard after the call, link in chat, but we have the key numbers here.
[00:25] Tom Ruiz: Great. We re-ran the ramp over the weekend and saw that queueing starts around the 900 concurrent token window.
[00:34] Marcus Li: Right, so to level-set: the weekend run simulated steady load up to 1200 tok/sec at average request length ~350 tokens. We used continuous batching with a 30ms batch accumulation window and concurrency set to 8 per worker.
[00:48] Sara Patel: That 30ms number — we had originally tried 20ms, correct? Seems like 30ms smoothed spikes better.
[00:55] Marcus Li: Yeah 20ms gave slightly lower p50 but p95 and p99 spiked because the batch build-up was too aggressive under burst. With 30ms we trade a bit of median latency for much lower tail.
[01:08] Jordan Miles: Do you have p95 numbers? We care about the 99th since our front-end SLA is strict.
[01:14] Marcus Li: Sure. Baseline for the quiet region: p50 ~ 60ms, p95 ~ 420ms, p99 ~ 780ms when under steady 600 tok/s. At 1200 tok/s with current config p50 ~ 110ms, p95 ~ 1.9s, p99 ~ 3.8s.
[01:28] Sara Patel: Oof, 3.8s is rough for our checkout flow if that happens during promos.
[01:33] Tom Ruiz: To add, we saw queue length ramp that caused CPU on the router to spike and then some requests had to be retried from our side which made the observed client retries confound the throughput metrics a bit.
[01:46] Marcus Li: Yep and that's the queue/backpressure interplay — once requests start queuing beyond the concurrency limit, the latency compounds. Two levers we discussed: increase concurrency per worker or reduce batch window. Both have cost/latency tradeoffs.
[01:58] Avery Kim: Also burst capacity — Dedicated burst nodes came into play when we flipped the burst toggle. We saw capacity handoffs but there was a 300-400ms warmup in the first 30s of the burst.
[02:12] Sara Patel: Warmup — is that model cold start or just queue warm-up?
[02:17] Marcus Li: Mostly KV cache and kernel scheduling where the runtime warms the token cache and fuse paths. Not a full model cold start, but you see slightly higher latency until the cache stabilizes.
[02:28] Tom Ruiz: For context our traffic pattern is very spiky: spikes of 90s during promos then back to baseline. So the warmup period is what breaks the UX.
[02:39] Marcus Li: Understood. One idea: canary a shorter batch window (20ms) on a fraction of capacity while enabling more aggressive burst nodes with pre-warmed cache. That uses a pinning strategy to keep a small pool always warm.
[02:55] Jordan Miles: Pinning sounds promising. What's the cost delta on pre-warmed pins?
[02:59] Avery Kim: We'll put numbers in the pricing sheet but ballpark it's an extra 10-15% on your Dedicated committed capacity depending on idle retention.
[03:10] Sara Patel: We want cost estimates tied to latency outcomes — like p95 improvements per cost percent.
[03:16] Marcus Li: Totally. We'll map cost vs latency across three configs: aggressive batching (20ms), balanced (30ms), and conservative (50ms) with concurrency 6/8/12 and with/without pinned warmers.
[03:30] Tom Ruiz: On concurrency, you said 8 per worker. If we bump to 12, what happens to token throughput per GPU?
[03:36] Marcus Li: It increases but with diminishing returns — more concurrency lets batching be more efficient but also increases memory pressure on KV cache. At 12 we saw ~8-12% more throughput but p99 worsened unless we also tuned the compile kernels and turned on a slightly different quantization path.
[03:53] Sara Patel: Quantization path — can you remind me which model variant we deployed?
[03:58] Marcus Li: It's an LLaMA-variant 70B quantized to q4_k_m (note: apologies if that transcript garbles the exact q-mode). The runtime has two execution paths; one is lower-memory but slightly slower for long sequences.
[04:13] Jordan Miles: Are those execution paths something we can switch dynamically?
[04:16] Marcus Li: Yes, the runtime can flip kernels per model variant and sequence profile, but switching has a small recompile cost (~100-200ms) so not ideal in the middle of big spikes.
[04:28] Tom Ruiz: Ok. What about queueing settings at the router — you mentioned moving to a queue length cap with backpressure signals.
[04:35] Marcus Li: Correct. We can set a hard queue cap to shed or return 429s early, or implement backpressure signaling so clients slow down. For your use-case I suggested a soft cap with exponential backoff on retries.
[04:48] Sara Patel: We prefer graceful degradation over hard failures. 429s during checkout would kill conversions.
[04:53] Marcus Li: In that case, soft cap plus pinning warmers is the least disruptive; we also recommend a client-side retry jitter and a fallback to a smaller model variant for non-critical calls.
[05:04] Avery Kim: Quick check — do you have any regulatory constraints that require keeping tokens or request logs beyond certain windows? It affects cache and retention.
[05:12] Sara Patel: We're fine keeping request metadata for 30 days; no PII in payloads.
[05:18] Marcus Li: Good — that makes KV caching straightforward.
[05:22] Tom Ruiz: Can you talk through the 3-day ramp configuration? What changed each day and what was stable?
[05:29] Marcus Li: Day 1 we tested baseline 600 tok/s. Day 2 we ramped to 900 tok/s with 30ms batching and concurrency 8. Day 3 we spiked to 1200 tok/s and toggled burst nodes for 2 10-minute promo windows.
[05:42] Sara Patel: The spreadsheet in the chat shows a weird blip on day 3 around 14:12 UTC where p95 doubled briefly. Any idea?
[05:50] Marcus Li: That corresponded to a client-side retry storm — some requests timed out at the client and retried creating a feedback loop. We flagged that in the trace.
[05:59] Jordan Miles: So observed p95 is a mix of server and client behaviors — we need to isolate.
[06:04] Marcus Li: Exactly. We recommend you re-run with client retry capped and jittered so we can see pure server-side tail behavior. That's part of the next run.
[06:13] Tom Ruiz: For the next run we will cap retries to 1 and add jitter.
[06:17] Sara Patel: Also want to test a 5k sequence long-tail run — will that surface any different behavior?
[06:24] Marcus Li: Yes long sequences stress KV cache and memory; for 5k sequences the batch size is smaller but each request is heavier. Expect throughput to drop per GPU and p99 to increase. We'll measure how quantization path affects that.
[06:36] Avery Kim: Marcus, can you talk about autoscaling policy tweaks? We had the baseline at CPU utilization + queue length.
[06:42] Marcus Li: We can tune scale triggers to be queue-aware: scale up at queue length > X for Y seconds, scale down only after cooldown of Z minutes to avoid flapping. Also add rate-based scaling using request tokens/sec * seq_len estimate.
[06:56] Tom Ruiz: What's a safe cooldown? We saw oscillation with 30s cooldown.
[07:01] Marcus Li: Suggest 3-5 minutes cooldown and a separate quick-burst lane that can take short bursts with pre-warmed GPUs. The quick-burst lane doesn't scale down as aggressively.
[07:12] Sara Patel: That sounds like the pinning idea — keep small number of warm GPUs.
[07:16] Marcus Li: Exactly.
[07:18] Jordan Miles: Any immediate action on the model side to reduce tail? Like limiting max tokens on requests?
[07:24] Marcus Li: You could cap request_len to 1k for interactive flows and route longer generative jobs to an offline queue. That reduces variability.
[07:32] Tom Ruiz: We'll need to update the routing config to split long-running jobs.
[07:36] Sara Patel: Are there changes you recommend to the client SDK?
[07:39] Marcus Li: Yes, add jittered retry, detect 5xx vs 429 and treat 429 as backoff signal, and include seq_len hint so server can pre-allocate.
[07:50] Avery Kim: We're sharing two artifacts after this call: the updated runbook and a cost/latency matrix. Marcus will prepare the runbook.
[07:58] Marcus Li: I'll post a proposed autoscale YAML and the burst policy. Also will include a small script to pre-warm the KV cache on pin nodes.
[08:08] Sara Patel: Thanks. One more question: how do we measure the UX impact for the checkout flow? Any A/B suggestion?
[08:14] Marcus Li: We recommend a canary where 10% of traffic uses the new config and we measure conversion delta and p95 latency. If conversion drops <1% and latency improves, roll further.
[08:27] Tom Ruiz: Sounds good. We'll set up a canary in our feature flagging system and coordinate times.
[08:32] Jordan Miles: Timeline — can we aim to have the next long-tail run by Dec 24? That's tight but doable.
[08:39] Sara Patel: We can try for Dec 24 if Redwood provides the autoscale playbook by Dec 22.
[08:46] Avery Kim: Confirmed, Marcus will have the playbook by Dec 22 and Avery will send the pricing sheet by Dec 20.
[08:54] Marcus Li: I'll also include a short checklist for the client retry cap and link to the trace filters we used.
[09:01] Sara Patel: Perfect. Anything else?
[09:04] Tom Ruiz: Nope from my side.
[09:06] Jordan Miles: Thanks all.
[09:07] Avery Kim: Thanks team. We'll follow up in the artifacts and lock dates.
[09:12] (chat) Marcus Li: Link: /drive/nimbus/pilot_metrics_dec18.csv and /drive/nimbus/autoscale_playbook_draft.md

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions around model q-mode and kernel names, speaker overlaps, and some timestamps approximate.

References/Shared artifacts: /drive/nimbus/pilot_metrics_dec18.csv, /drive/nimbus/autoscale_playbook_draft.md, pricing_sheet_nimbus_v2.xlsx
